title: Intel sued by shareholders over alleged concealment of PC sales slowdown impact
text:
Intel sued by shareholders over alleged concealment of PC sales slowdown impact | Lianhe Zaobao 
 Singapore International China Business Opinion Lifestyle Entertainment Search Published / 16 Nov 2026 10:10 S M L XL Intel sued by shareholders over alleged concealment of PC sales slowdown impact
 AI-translated article with transliterated names. Read original Chinese article here. 
 Intel shares plunged 28.6% on 30 October. A day earlier, the company had forecast fourth-quarter revenue and earnings below market expectations and projected a prolonged slowdown in personal computer sales. （Reuters file picture） Intel has been sued by shareholders who allege it concealed the impact of a prolonged slowdown in personal computer sales and a build-up of inventory on revenue, causing its shares to plunge nearly 29% on 30 October and wiping out about US$140 billion (S$180 billion) in market value in a day. 
 Reuters reported that shareholders led by a Michigan pension fund filed a class-action lawsuit last Friday (13 November) in federal court in San Jose, California. They accused Intel of failing to disclose promptly the impact that slowing PC sales and excess inventory would have on revenue. 
 The shareholders said problems in the PC business and the negative impact of excess inventory outweighed the benefits of data centre construction and other developments driven by the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. 
 They also alleged that Intel’s sale of US$23 billion worth of shares at US$95 apiece in mid-August, halfway through its “disastrous” third quarter, showed that the company had the motive and opportunity to deceive investors. 
 Intel was then seeking to expand its chip foundry business, a central part of chief executive Lip-Bu Tan’s business strategy. Intel shares closed at US$59.66 last Friday. 
 Intel did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on Sunday (15 November). 
 Intel shares plunged 28.6% on 30 October. A day earlier, the company had forecast fourth-quarter revenue and earnings below market expectations and projected a prolonged slowdown in personal computer sales. 
 Tan told analysts at the time that he was disappointed by supply shortages in manufacturing, while an “unprecedented memory shortage” was weakening demand in the personal computer market. 
 “We must address these challenges with urgency,” he said. 
 Like many large technology companies, Intel has invested heavily in expanding manufacturing capacity in recent years, but supply disruptions have made it harder for the company to benefit from growing demand for data centre chips. Meanwhile, rising memory prices have pushed up PC prices, further dampening demand. 
 The lawsuit, led by the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System, seeks unspecified damages on behalf of shareholders who bought Intel shares between 23 July and 29 October 2026. Tan and chief financial officer David Zinsner were also named as defendants. 
 Despite retreating from a recent high of US$142.35 reached on 30 June, Intel shares were still up 62% for the year as of last Friday.
